source.title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
source.authors: Jason Wei; Yi Tay; Rishi Bommasani; Colin A. Raffel; Barret Zoph; Sebastian Borgeaud; Dani Yogatama; Maarten Bosma; Denny Zhou; Donald Metzler; Ed H. Chi; Tatsunori B. Hashimoto; O. Vinyals; P. Liang; J. Dean; W. Fedus

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper's own analysis finds downstream benchmark metrics that remain near random at smaller scales and then rise at larger scales, challenging the predictability of downstream performance from smaller runs. Its cross-entropy analysis concerns task targets, not held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own Appendix A.1 analysis of six LaMDA BIG-Bench tasks. Other scaling curves and examples discussed in the paper are primarily surveyed from cited work and are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The paper is mostly a survey of others' scaling curves. Its own analyses (Appendix A.1–A.3) bear on V6. On six LaMDA BIG-Bench tasks, downstream metrics stay near random up to about 1e22 FLOPs and then jump, while task-target cross-entropy improves throughout. In A.3 the authors classify all BIG-Bench tasks as smooth, emergent or flat. The paper does not fit held-out pretraining-loss laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors' main claim is that some abilities are absent in smaller models and present in larger ones, so they cannot be predicted by extrapolating smaller models' performance. Their appendix analyses find that task cross-entropy improves where metrics are flat, and that emergence persists across partial-credit metrics. Neither analysis explains or predicts when emergence occurs.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes few-shot downstream BIG-Bench metrics and task-target cross-entropy across LaMDA scales; it does not fit held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The apparent scaling pattern depends on the evaluation metric: task-target cross-entropy improves at scales where exact match, BLEU, or accuracy is close to random. The generative-task error plots also show both greedy decoding (T=0) and random sampling (T=1).
record.problems: The evidence is limited to six few-shot BIG-Bench tasks on LaMDA; most plotted values are not numerically reported in the text. The logical arguments task has only 32 samples, which the paper notes may contribute to noise. Task-target cross-entropy is not held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible own-result rows left out. Scaling examples elsewhere in the paper are surveyed from cited studies and were not entered as this study's results.

untested.parts: All: no held-out pretraining-loss power-law fits.
All: no extrapolation of fitted loss laws.
All: no depth/width ablations at fixed parameter count.
All: no other modalities or training regimes tested.
Prediction of downstream performance from held-out pretraining loss. The WikiText103-perplexity plot (Fig. 4) uses cited Gopher/Chinchilla results, not the study's own.
All: no exponent fitting or fitting-choice comparisons.

missing.what: The study's own classification of BIG-Bench tasks into smoothly increasing, emergent with LaMDA/GPT-3, emergent with PaLM, flat, and other, with per-keyword proportions
Emergence on three generative tasks persists across all BIG-Bench metrics, including partial-credit BLEU, ROUGE and BLEURT
Log-probabilities of correct and incorrect responses both fall with scale, then diverge at the emergence scale
PaLM 62B is above random on 14 BIG-Bench tasks where LaMDA 137B and GPT-3 175B are near random, so emergence depends on more than scale

record.verdict_notes: Most of the paper's scaling curves (Figs 2–4, Table 1) come from cited work. Only the Appendix A analyses are the study's own results. The six-task rows come from a sample selected for emergence, so they show that unpredictable cases exist, not how often they occur. The A.3 classification is the frequency evidence and is unrowed.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute, and power-law fits over several orders of magnitude.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities and training regimes.
The analysis covers six few-shot BIG-Bench tasks on LaMDA, not downstream tasks generally or the predictive relationship to held-out pretraining loss.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal allocation, and whether choices such as parameter counting, training schedule, data, or fitting method alter scaling-law fits.

relationships.condition: Six LaMDA few-shot BIG-Bench tasks selected as emergent, measured with downstream metrics (EM, BLEU, accuracy)
relationships.reason: Performance stays near random up to ≤1e22 FLOPs/27B parameters, then jumps, so it is not predictable from smaller models. These tasks were chosen because they are emergent (r1, r2, r4, r5, r7, r8, r10, r12, r14).
relationships.display_finding: Performance remained near random through scales up to 1e22 FLOPs and 27B parameters before jumping on six tasks selected for emergence.

relationships.condition: Task-target cross-entropy on the same six tasks
relationships.reason: Task log-likelihood improves smoothly where metrics are flat, but shows an elbow at emergence. The authors say it gives no straightforward way to predict emergence (r3, r6, r9, r11, r13, r15).
relationships.display_finding: Task log-likelihood improves smoothly while task metrics remain flat, then develops an elbow at emergence without providing a straightforward prediction of that emergence.

relationships.condition: All BIG-Bench tasks classified in Appendix A.3/E (no rows)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows. Many tasks scale smoothly, while many others are emergent or flat, so predictable improvement holds only for a subset of tasks.
relationships.display_finding: Many BIG-Bench tasks improve smoothly, while many others exhibit abrupt emergence or remain flat.

reader_labels.reason: Smaller models are described as near random before metrics rise at an emergence scale, so smaller-scale performance does not straightforwardly predict the later downstream result (r1, r2, r4, r5, r7, r8, r10, r12, r14).
